facts.statement: California sea lions are eared seals from the West Coast of North America.
facts.quote: California sea lions are “eared seals” native to the West Coast of North America.

facts.statement: Visible ear flaps set sea lions apart from true seals.
facts.quote: Their visible ear flaps distinguish them from true seals.

facts.statement: True seals have ear holes but no outer ear flap.
facts.quote: belong to a group of pinnipeds that have ear holes but lack an external ear flap

facts.statement: Sea lions belong to the walking seal family and use large flippers to walk on land.
facts.quote: As a member of the otariid or “walking seal” family, California sea lions have large flippers that they use to walk on land.

facts.statement: Their loud roars and barks help explain the name sea lion.
facts.quote: Sea lions produce loud roars and barking, which helps explain why they're named after lions.

facts.statement: California sea lions do not have a mane.
facts.quote: California sea lions lack the "mane" that gives sea lions their name.

facts.statement: California sea lions are playful, clever and very noisy, sounding like barking dogs.
facts.quote: California sea lions are playful, intelligent, and very vocal (sounding like barking dogs).

facts.statement: Females grow to about 6 feet long and males to about 7.5 feet.
facts.quote: 6 feet (females) to 7.5 feet (males)

facts.statement: Females weigh about 240 pounds and males up to about 700 pounds.
facts.quote: 240 pounds (females) to 700 pounds (males)

facts.statement: Males reach 600 to 850 pounds and 7 feet; females 200 to 250 pounds and up to 6 feet.
facts.quote: male sea lions are much larger—reaching up to 600 to 850 pounds and 7 feet in length. Females grow to 200 to 250 pounds and up to 6 feet in length.

facts.statement: Males reach almost 8 feet and more than 600 pounds; females up to 6.5 feet and 240 pounds.
facts.quote: Male California sea lions reach lengths of almost 8 feet in length, and weights of more than 600 pounds. Females, may reach up to 6 and a half feet in length and weigh up to 240 pounds.

facts.statement: A newborn pup is about 2.5 feet (75 cm) long.
facts.quote: Pups are about 2.5 feet (75 centimeters) long, nose to tail tip, and weigh about 18 pounds (8 kilograms) at birth.

facts.statement: Newborn pups weigh 13 to 20 pounds.
facts.quote: Newborn California sea lions weigh 13 to 20 pounds

facts.statement: Pups weigh about 16 pounds at birth.
facts.quote: Pups are dark brown at birth and weigh about 16 pounds.

facts.statement: Their bodies are torpedo shaped and taper to the tail, with strong bulky shoulders.
facts.quote: They have strong, bulky shoulders and their streamlined, torpedo-shaped bodies taper to the tail.

facts.statement: They have a slender neck and a dog-like head.
facts.quote: They also have a more slender neck than some species and a dog-like head.

facts.statement: In both sexes the muzzle is long and dog-like, tapering to a fairly blunt end.
facts.quote: In both sexes, the muzzle is dog-like and long, slightly tapering to a moderately blunt end.

facts.statement: They have broad front flippers and long, narrow snouts.
facts.quote: California sea lions have broad front flippers and long, narrow snouts.

facts.statement: They have visible ear flaps on each side of the head.
facts.quote: The species has visible ear pinnae (ear flaps) on either side of its head

facts.statement: The ear flaps are small, but the sea lion hears well above and below water.
facts.quote: Though the sea lion's ear flaps are small, it can hear quite well both above and below the surface.

facts.statement: The ears close under water.
facts.quote: Its ears are also valvular and close underwater.

facts.statement: The front flippers are especially long and push the sea lion through the water.
facts.quote: Their front flippers are especially long and are used for propelling them through the water.

facts.statement: The front flippers are large and wing-like, with the bone structure of a land animal.
facts.quote: A California sea lions fore flippers are large and winglike, with the skeletal structure of a land animal.

verified.note: Statement repaired by second reader; was: "The front flippers are large and wing-like, with finger bones extended by cartilage."

facts.statement: The back flippers act as rudders and have three claws for grooming.
facts.quote: Their back flippers are used as rudders and have three claws for grooming.

facts.statement: They have three to five claws on their hind flippers.
facts.quote: three to five claws on their hind flippers

facts.statement: A small flat tail sits between the hind flippers.
facts.quote: The California sea lion has a small flattened tail between the hind flippers.

facts.statement: A thick layer of blubber just under the skin keeps the body warm and streamlined.
facts.quote: California sea lions deposit most of their body fat into a thick layer of blubber just under the skin. The blubber layer insulates the California sea lion and streamlines the body.

verified.note: Second reader widened the quote with the sentence before it, copied from the open page, so it carries "thick" and "under the skin" used in the text.

facts.statement: Adult males are mostly dark brown to black.
facts.quote: Adult males are generally larger than females and are mostly dark brown to black in color.

facts.statement: Adult females and young are slender and blonde to tan.
facts.quote: Adult females and juveniles are slender-bodied and are blonde to tan in color.

facts.statement: Males are usually dark chestnut brown, some lighter on the head, sides and belly.
facts.quote: Males are generally a dark chestnut brown, although some males have lighter coloring on their head, muzzle, sides, hind and belly.

facts.statement: Colour varies; many males stay sandy brown on the sides, belly and rear.
facts.quote: many males do not darken completely, remaining sandy brown on the sides, belly, and rear quarters.

facts.statement: On most males the crest and parts of the muzzle and around the eyes get lighter with age.
facts.quote: On most males, especially darker individuals, the crest and a corresponding area on the muzzle and around the eyes lighten with age.

facts.statement: The crests of males are topped with tufts of blonde or lighter hair.
facts.quote: Subadult and adult males have pronounced forehead crests crowned with tufts of blonde or lighter hair.

facts.statement: All sea lions have dark, almost bare flippers.
facts.quote: All ages and sexes have contrasting black flippers, naked except for a short stubble of dark fur partially covering the upper surface.

facts.statement: Pups are born with a thick brownish black coat.
facts.quote: Pups are born with a thick brownish black lanugo that is generally molted by the end of the first month.

facts.statement: At 4 to 5 months pups swap their dark coat for a light brown or silver one.
facts.quote: When pups are 4 to 5 months old, they molt their dark brown coats for light brown or silver coats.

facts.statement: Their whiskers can turn forward and feel the small movements of nearby fish, even in total darkness.
facts.quote: Their sensitive whiskers, called vibrissae, can rotate forward and detect the slight movements of fish swimming nearby, enabling California sea lions to find and capture prey in total darkness.

facts.statement: Their eyesight is good because they spend a lot of time in dim water.
facts.quote: Their eyesight is well developed, because they spend a lot of time underwater with reduced light levels.

facts.statement: Mothers find their own pup by its call and then smell it to be sure.
facts.quote: A female can locate her pup among hundreds of others by her pup’s vocalization. When she finds her pup, she smells it as a final check.

facts.statement: They eat squid, anchovies, mackerel, rockfish and sardines.
facts.quote: They eat a variety of prey—such as squid, anchovies, mackerel, rockfish, and sardines—found in upwelling areas.

facts.statement: They eat squid, octopus and small schooling fish like herring, anchovies and sardines.
facts.quote: California sea lions feed on squid, octopus and small schooling fish like herring, anchovies and sardines.

facts.statement: Most of their food is in shallow water, about 26 to 74 m deep.
facts.quote: most of their food is found in shallow waters, about 26 to 74 m (85–243 ft.) deep.

facts.statement: In water they paddle with their front flippers and steer with the rear flippers like a rudder.
facts.quote: In the water, they propel themselves by paddling their front flippers and use their rear flippers to help steer, like a boat’s rudder.

facts.statement: Sea lions push themselves through the water by paddling their front flippers, and use their back flippers to help steer.
facts.quote: In the water, they propel themselves by paddling their front flippers and use their rear flippers to help steer, like a boat’s rudder.
facts.note: Quote seen in the search result abstract text; the article page itself did not open through the extract tool. A second reader should open it.

verified.note: Repaired: source swapped from feldkamp to noaaseal. The Feldkamp paper (journal page, PDF, DOI, PubMed) would not open on 2026-11-23. Statement cut back: NOAA does not say the thrust comes solely from the front flippers.

facts.statement: Sea lions swim with up and down, wing-like strokes of their front flippers.
facts.quote: Sea lions swim with up-and-down, wing-like strokes of their foreflippers.

facts.statement: On land they turn their hind flippers under the body and walk on all four flippers.
facts.quote: On land, these sea lions move by rotating their rear flippers under their bodies and supporting their body weight on all four flippers.

facts.statement: On land sea lions walk on their front flippers and their rear flippers turned under the body.
facts.quote: On land, sea lions use their large, elongated front flippers and rear flippers rotated underneath their bodies to “walk.”

facts.statement: True seals move on land on their bellies, like a caterpillar.
facts.quote: On land, seals use their bellies to move around in a caterpillar-like motion.

facts.statement: True seals swim mainly with their back flippers, while sea lions use their front flippers.
facts.quote: They also use their fore flippers to propel themselves through the water, whereas true seals rely primarily on their back flippers to swim.
facts.note: Added by the second reader (quote copied from the open page): the text says this and the ledger quoted it, but no dossier fact carried it. Needs a different reader to verify.

verified.note: Quote found letter for letter on the National Zoo page (advanced extract, 2026-11-23).

facts.statement: True seals swim by moving their back flippers back and forth, like a fish uses its tail.
facts.quote: In the water, seals swim easily, moving their rear flippers back and forth, similar to how a fish uses its caudal fin (tail) to propel itself through the water.
facts.note: Added by the second reader (quote copied from the open page): the text says this and the ledger quoted it, but no dossier fact carried it. Needs a different reader to verify.

verified.note: Quote found letter for letter on the NOAA Fisheries page (advanced extract, 2026-11-23).

facts.statement: They are sometimes seen porpoising, jumping out of the water, probably to swim faster.
facts.quote: They are sometimes seen porpoising, or jumping out of the water, presumably to speed up their swimming.

facts.statement: They can reach 25 to 30 mph (40 to 48 km/h).
facts.quote: they can quickly reach speeds of 25-30 mph (40-48 kph) while hunting, avoiding predators or simply playing.

facts.statement: California sea lions can swim at 25 miles per hour.
facts.quote: California sea lions are very fast swimmers, reaching speeds of 25 miles per hour!

facts.statement: The deepest dive recorded was 900 feet and lasted just under ten minutes.
facts.quote: The deepest dive ever recorded by this species was 900 feet and it lasted just under ten minutes.

facts.statement: They usually stay under water 3 minutes or less, at most about 10 minutes.
facts.quote: California sea lions usually stay submerged three minutes or less; however, they can remain submerged for as long as 10 minutes.

facts.statement: Rafting sea lions hold their flippers above the water to rest and to warm or cool off.
facts.quote: A rafting sea lion holds its flippers above the water for a long time, motionless, to rest and regulate its body temperature.

facts.statement: They rest packed together on land or float together in groups called rafts.
facts.quote: groups often rest closely packed together at favorite haul-out sites on land or float together on the ocean's surface in groups called "rafts."

facts.statement: They gather in groups of a thousand or more on land.
facts.quote: California sea lions are among the most gregarious marine mammals, forming dense aggregations of a thousand or more animals on land.

facts.statement: Males bark like dogs to talk to other males and to females.
facts.quote: California sea lion males bark like dogs to communicate with other males and females.

facts.statement: Males bark on land and sometimes even under water.
facts.quote: Males typically patrol their aquatic and terrestrial territories and bark or roar to warn intruders away — sometimes even barking underwater.

facts.statement: Sea lions are known for their loud, clear bark.
facts.quote: Sea lions can be noisy and are easily recognizable by their loud and distinct “bark.”

facts.statement: Each mother and pup have calls that are their own.
facts.quote: Females and pups communicate using vocalizations that are unique to the female and pup.

facts.statement: Most pups are born in June or July.
facts.quote: Most pups are born in June or July and weigh 13 to 20 pounds.

facts.statement: A mother gives birth to one pup.
facts.quote: Females give birth to a single pup

verified.note: Statement repaired by second reader; was: "A mother has one pup at a time."

facts.statement: A mother nurses her pup 1 to 2 days, then feeds at sea 2 to 5 days and comes back.
facts.quote: A mother sea lion nurses her pup for 1 to 2 days, then leaves the pup ashore while she travels to feeding areas at sea. She spends 2 to 5 days feeding, then returns to nurse.

facts.statement: Pups stay with their mother for about a year, learning to swim and find food.
facts.quote: stay with their mother for about a year as they nurse and learn important survival skills, like how to swim and find food on their own.

facts.statement: From about 4 years old males grow a bony bump on the skull, fully grown by 7.
facts.quote: starting at 4 years old, males develop a bony bump on top of their skull known as a sagittal crest, which is fully developed by 7 years old.

facts.statement: They live 20 to 30 years.
facts.quote: 20 to 30 years

facts.statement: In the wild they can live up to 17 years; one in human care lived over 31.
facts.quote: In the wild this species can live up to 17 years, although in captivity, one California sea lion lived over 31 years.

facts.statement: At about 5 years old males grow a crest along the top of the skull, giving a high domed forehead.
facts.quote: At about 5 years old, males develop a noticeable crest that runs lengthwise along the top of their skull creating a high, domed forehead.

facts.statement: Grown males have a raised forehead crest that grows to about an inch and a half by ten years old.
facts.quote: Mature adult males have a raised forehead called the sagittal crest which increases to about an inch and a half at ten years of age.

verified.note: Statement repaired by second reader; was: "Grown males have a raised forehead crest about an inch and a half high by ten years; females have none."

facts.statement: Females have no big crest and a thinner head that slopes gently to the muzzle.
facts.quote: Females lack a pronounced crest and have a thinner head that slopes more gently to the end of the muzzle.

facts.statement: Adult males are much bigger and sturdier than females.
facts.quote: Adult males are substantially more robust and larger than females.

facts.statement: Sea lions are grown up enough to breed at 4 to 5 years old.
facts.quote: Sea lions reach sexual maturity at 4 to 5 years old

facts.statement: Females can breed at about 3 years, males at 5.
facts.quote: Female California sea lions reach sexual maturity around 3 years of age, whereas males are sexually mature at 5 years old.

facts.statement: They live in coastal waters and on beaches, docks, buoys and jetties.
facts.quote: They live in coastal waters and on beaches, docks, buoys, and jetties.

facts.statement: They live in the shallow waters of the eastern North Pacific.
facts.quote: California sea lions live in the shallow waters of the eastern North Pacific Ocean.

facts.statement: They like sandy beaches or rocky coves to breed and rest.
facts.quote: They prefer sandy beaches or rocky coves for breeding and haul-out sites.

facts.statement: IUCN gives a lower depth limit of 400 metres.
facts.quote:
Lower depth limit

400 metres
facts.note: Table cells on the IUCN page.

verified.note: The page also shows Population trend: Increasing, and says this is not the latest assessment for this species.

facts.statement: They range from southeast Alaska to central Mexico.
facts.quote: California sea lions range from southeast Alaska to the Pacific coast of central Mexico.

facts.statement: They mainly breed from the Channel Islands in southern California to central Mexico.
facts.quote: Their primary breeding range is from the Channel Islands in southern California to central Mexico.

facts.statement: San Miguel Island has one of the biggest sea lion breeding beaches in the world.
facts.quote: San Miguel Island is home to one of the largest rookeries in the world for California sea lions with a breeding population of approximately 80,000 animals.

facts.statement: The IUCN lists the California sea lion as Least Concern (2014 assessment).
facts.quote: Zalophus californianus is listed as Least Concern.

verified.note: The page also shows Population trend: Increasing, and says this is not the latest assessment for this species. Statement repaired by second reader; was: "The IUCN lists the California sea lion as Least Concern with a rising population (2014 assessment)."

facts.statement: Their numbers have grown since at least 1975, after they were protected.
facts.quote: Their population has been increasing since at least 1975, after protections were put in place under the MMPA.

facts.statement: Orcas and great white sharks eat sea lions.
facts.quote: sea lions are preyed upon by orca whales and great white sharks

facts.statement: If you see a pup on the shore, leave it be.
facts.quote: If you see a pup on the shore, please leave it be.

verified.note: Statement repaired by second reader; was: "If you see a pup alone on the shore, leave it be; its mother is likely feeding at sea."

facts.statement: The recording comes from a group of about 100 sea lions on a sandy beach at Channel Islands Harbor, Ventura County, California, in January 2023.
facts.quote: A colony of Sea Lions reaching approximately 100+ or more were gathering together on this sandy area of Kiddie Beach @ the S.E. end of Channel Islands Harbor.
facts.note: Read through api.inaturalist.org/v1/observations/145868221 (the description field); the observation page itself is not reachable by curl. Observed 2023-01-03, research grade.

facts.statement: Males, females, pups and young sea lions were all in that group.
facts.quote: Both male & female, pups, juveniles & adults sleeping, resting, gregariously active & playing.
facts.note: From the observation description via the iNaturalist API.

gaps.note: No source opened here explains how the bark is made (larynx, air flow). The text says only that they bark.
No source gives exact proportions (flipper length to body length, head length). The model proportions are an estimate from the sources' words: long front flippers, torpedo body, dog-like head.
No source describes how high or how far a porpoising leap goes. The animation height is our own choice.
Animal Diversity Web says they echolocate; no agency or aquarium page opened here says so. Left out of the text.

conflicts.note: Male length 7.5 ft (NOAA), 7 ft (TMMC), almost 8 ft (NPS); male weight 700 lb (NOAA), 600 to 850 lb (TMMC), more than 600 lb (NPS). Text uses the NOAA quick facts and says "about".
Three claws (Smithsonian) or three to five (NOAA). Text avoids a number.
Deepest recorded dive 274 m / 900 ft (NPS, SeaWorld) but IUCN gives 400 m as the lower depth limit. animal.json max uses 274.
Top speed 25 to 30 mph (Smithsonian) or 25 mph (TMMC); SeaWorld says probably 21.6 km/h (13.4 mph). Text does not give a speed.
Lifespan 20 to 30 years (NOAA) vs up to 17 in the wild (NPS). Text does not give a lifespan.
Female maturity 3 (TMMC) or 4 to 5 years (NOAA); crest starts at 4 (TMMC) or about 5 (Smithsonian). Text says "as they grow up".
Pup weight 13 to 20 lb (TMMC, NPS), about 16 lb (NOAA), about 18 lb (Smithsonian). All agree in range.
NPS says the dark birth coat is shed by the end of the first month; NOAA says pups molt their dark brown coats at 4 to 5 months. Not in the text.
